name: Uranium sand house

card.summary: Mid-century radioactive sand rooms where visitors sat on mildly radioactive sand, promoted for joint pain and general rejuvenation.
card.aka: Radioactive sand baths, uranium sand therapy
card.note: Radiation exposure carries documented health risks; a historical practice documented in the 1950s.

quick.overview:
Uranium sand houses were round rooms with benches over a floor of mildly radioactive sand, usually beach sand mixed with crushed minerals such as carnotite, a uranium-bearing mineral. Operators in the American Southwest promoted sessions as therapy for arthritis, bursitis and rheumatism.

They belong to a wider early and mid-20th-century wave of radioactive health products and spas, which also included radon spas and radium drinks. Their link to appearance is the same promise made by those wellness fads: comfort, vitality and a healthier, younger look. No sand-house outcomes have been published in medical journals.
quick.how: Historical descriptions say clients sat in a round room on benches, or lay in a narrow box of sand said to contain uranium ore, for a session. This wiki gives no instructions.
quick.risks: Ionizing radiation exposure is associated with documented harms, and regulators have warned about radioactive consumer products. Radium products of the same era, such as Radithor, were linked to deaths, including that of industrialist Eben Byers in 1932.

lead: A uranium sand house was a commercial therapy room popular in Utah, New Mexico and Colorado during the 1950s. Patients sat on benches in a round room whose floor was mildly radioactive sand, usually beach sand mixed with crushed minerals such as carnotite.[1]

A related treatment had people lie in a narrow box of sand said to contain uranium ore, promoted for arthritis, bursitis and rheumatism as late as 1956, according to a Miami News report titled 'Clinic Plugs Uranium Sand Cures.'[1] Radioactive health products of this kind promised pain relief and renewed vigor, and radon spas and health mines are the modern descendants.[1]
Sand houses appear in encyclopedic coverage of radioactive quackery. No clinical trials of them are known.

angle.text: Operators promoted the sand rooms for joint pain and rejuvenation. Any appearance benefit was part of a general wellness promise rather than a specific cosmetic claim.

paras: The sand house was a round room with benches over a floor of mildly radioactive sand.[1] Carnotite is a bright yellow uranium potassium vanadate mineral mined in the Colorado Plateau region.[1]

Radioactivity was discovered in 1896, and radioactive products were most popular in the early 20th century, including Radithor (late 1920s) and the Radiendocrinator (about 1924-1929).[1] Radon spas in Joachimsthal (now Jachymov) date from 1906, and similar spas still operate in Germany, Ukraine, Belarus and Austria, where German statutory insurance covers visits.[1] Sand houses were part of the 1950s boom in the American Southwest alongside radon-water devices.[1]

Regulators such as the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission have warned that some products containing uranium or thorium had radiation levels high enough to require licensing.[1] A review in the research literature has said that limited experimental and anecdotal evidence suggests low radiation doses from radon spas and monazite sands might be useful for some inflammatory conditions, and calls for more study; it does not examine uranium sand houses.[2]
Radium products of the era produced documented fatalities, such as that of Eben Byers in 1932 after he consumed Radithor heavily between 1927 and 1930.[1]
No studies found. Related research on radon spas and low-dose radiation exists but does not concern uranium sand houses.[2]
